title: Skeletal and muscular system
summary: How does the skeleton carry us, and how do muscles contract?
cards.0.p: The skeleton supports the body, protects the organs and, together with the muscles, makes movement possible. Blood cells are made in red marrow. Bones also store calcium and phosphorus.
cards.0.key: An adult human has about 206 bones. The rib cage protects the heart and lungs, and the spine protects the spinal cord.
cards.0.once.soru: What is the main job of the skull?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: The skull is a hard box around the brain.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Blood cells are made in the red marrow inside bones.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: The skull bones are joined by immovable joints and do not move.
cards.1.p: Cartilage is a flexible supporting tissue. Its cells, the chondrocytes, live in spaces in the matrix. Cartilage has no blood vessels, and nutrients arrive by diffusion. That is why cartilage heals slowly.
cards.1.svg#15: chondrocytes in lacunae · no blood vessels
cards.1.key: The space where a cartilage cell sits is called a lacuna. Hyaline cartilage is found on joint surfaces and in the trachea, elastic cartilage in the outer ear, and fibrous cartilage in the discs between the vertebrae.
cards.1.once.soru: Why does damaged cartilage in the knee heal so slowly?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: Nutrients arrive slowly by diffusion, so repair is slow too.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: Cartilage does have cells, the chondrocytes.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: Cartilage is flexible. It heals slowly because it has no blood vessels.
cards.2.p: The shaft of a long bone is called the diaphysis, and it is made of compact bone. In its middle is the marrow cavity. The ends are called epiphyses, and they are made of spongy bone. The periosteum that covers the bone repairs fractures.
cards.2.key: Compact bone gives strength, and spongy bone keeps the bone light. The periosteum makes the bone thicker. The joint surfaces are covered with cartilage.
cards.2.etk.soru: Tap the parts of the long bone.
cards.2.etk.noktalar.0.acik: Articular cartilage covers the ends of the bone. It reduces friction in the joint and cushions impact.
cards.2.etk.noktalar.1.acik: Spongy bone is the porous bone in the epiphysis. Its spaces hold red marrow, which makes blood cells.
cards.2.etk.noktalar.2.acik: As cartilage cells in the growth plate divide and turn into bone, the bone grows longer. This plate turns to bone at the end of puberty.
cards.2.etk.noktalar.3.acik: The periosteum is the membrane that covers the bone. It carries blood vessels and nerves, makes the bone thicker and repairs fractures.
cards.2.etk.noktalar.4.acik: Compact bone is the thick, hard wall of the diaphysis. It is made of Haversian systems.
cards.2.etk.noktalar.5.acik: The marrow cavity is in the middle of the diaphysis. In adults it is mostly filled with yellow marrow, which stores fat.
cards.2.once.soru: Which structure repairs a broken bone?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: The periosteum is the membrane that covers the bone. It carries blood vessels, nerves and bone-building cells.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: Articular cartilage covers the ends of the bone and does not repair fractures.
cards.3.p: Red marrow makes red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Yellow marrow is mostly fat. With age, the marrow in the shafts of long bones turns yellow.
cards.3.svg#14: after heavy blood loss, yellow marrow can turn red
cards.3.key: In adults, red marrow remains in the flat bones, the vertebrae, the hips and the ends of the long bones.
cards.3.once.soru: What color is the marrow in a baby's long bones?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: In babies almost all the marrow is red, and it turns yellow with age.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: Marrow is either red or yellow.
cards.4.p: Compact bone is made of Haversian systems, and the canal in the middle of each system holds blood vessels and nerves. Osteoblasts build bone and then become osteocytes. Osteoclasts break bone down.
cards.4.key: You can remember osteoBlasts as "builders" and osteoClasts as "crushers". The matrix of bone is made of calcium phosphate and collagen.
cards.4.once.soru: Is bone a living tissue that is constantly renewed?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: Bone cells constantly build new bone and break down old bone.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: Building and breakdown go on in bone throughout life.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: Bone is constantly renewed in adults too.
cards.5.h: Types of bone and growth in length
cards.5.p: There are three kinds of bone: long bones like the thigh bone, short bones like the wrist bones and flat bones like the skull bones. A long bone grows longer as the cartilage in its growth plate divides and turns to bone.
cards.5.svg#12: closes at the end of puberty
cards.5.key: Flat bones turn to bone from a membrane, and long bones from a cartilage model. Too much GH causes gigantism before the plate closes and acromegaly after it closes.
cards.6.p: Immovable joints, like those in the skull, do not move at all. Slightly movable joints, like those between the vertebrae, move a little. In movable joints, the bone ends glide thanks to synovial fluid, and ligaments hold the bones together.
cards.6.key: Ligaments connect bone to bone, and tendons connect muscle to bone.
cards.7.p: Skeletal muscle is striated and works under our control. Smooth muscle is not striated and works involuntarily. It is found in the walls of the stomach and blood vessels. Cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary, and its cells are linked by intercalated discs.
cards.7.key: Skeletal muscle cells have many nuclei. Smooth muscle contracts slowly, but it can stay contracted for hours while using little ATP.
cards.7.etk.soru: Put each example or feature under the right type of muscle.
cards.7.etk.ogeler.1.2: The diaphragm is a skeletal muscle that drives breathing. You can control it if you want, by holding your breath.
cards.8.p: Skeletal muscle is made of long muscle fibers, each fiber is made of myofibrils, and each myofibril is made of sarcomeres. The regular arrangement of thin actin and thick myosin filaments makes the muscle look striated.
cards.8.key: A sarcomere is the section between two Z lines. The A band is as long as the myosin. The light region in its middle that holds only myosin is called the H zone.
cards.8.once.soru: What makes muscle look striated under a microscope?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: When thick and thin filaments line up regularly, light and dark bands form.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: Nuclei do not form the stripes.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: Blood vessels do not form regular bands.
cards.9.p: During contraction the filaments do not shorten. They slide past each other. Acetylcholine stimulates the muscle membrane, and Ca²⁺ ions are released. This opens the binding sites on actin. Then the myosin heads pull on actin using the energy of ATP.
cards.9.svg#3: Z lines move closer, actin and myosin keep their length
cards.9.key: The Ca²⁺ ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Poisons such as curare block the action of acetylcholine, and the muscle cannot contract.
cards.10.p: Muscle contracts only with ATP, and the ready supply of ATP lasts a few seconds. Creatine phosphate quickly renews ATP. After that comes aerobic respiration, and if there is not enough oxygen, lactic acid fermentation.
cards.10.key: A sprinter relies on creatine phosphate and fermentation, and a marathon runner relies on aerobic respiration. The buildup of lactic acid also adds to muscle fatigue.
cards.11.p: A single stimulus causes a brief contraction. This is called a twitch. If stimuli come one after another, the contractions add up and the muscle stays contracted without a break. This is called tetanus. When ATP runs low, the muscle's force drops. This is called fatigue.
cards.11.svg#9: force drops in a tired muscle
cards.11.key: The phases of a twitch are the latent period, contraction and relaxation. Muscle tetanus is not the same as the disease tetanus.
cards.11.once.soru: What happens if you stimulate a muscle again and again without letting it relax?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: The contractions pile up and the muscle contracts without a break.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: For the muscle to relax, the stimuli have to stop.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: Separate twitches need time to relax between stimuli.
cards.12.h: Types of contraction and the motor unit
cards.12.p: A motor neuron and the muscle fibers it stimulates are called a motor unit. If many units are stimulated, the muscle contracts strongly. In an isotonic contraction the muscle shortens, and in an isometric contraction its length does not change.
cards.12.svg#3: eye muscle: few fibers per neuron
cards.12.svg#10: length stays the same (pushing a wall)
cards.12.key: In eye and finger muscles, one neuron stimulates only a few fibers. This is what allows fine movements. An isometric contraction also uses ATP.
cards.12.once.soru: You push a wall with all your strength, and it does not move. Are your muscles contracting?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: The muscle tenses and uses ATP, but its length does not change.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: If your muscles were not contracting, you could not push at all.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: Because the wall does not move, the length of your arm does not change.
cards.13.p: Muscles can only pull, not push. That is why there are antagonistic pairs of muscles that work against each other. For example, when the biceps contracts the arm bends and the triceps relaxes. The slight tension in a resting muscle is called muscle tone.
cards.13.key: The biceps is a flexor, and the triceps is an extensor. Muscle tone keeps our posture.
cards.14.p: In osteoporosis, bone density drops and bones break easily. Vitamin D, made in the skin with sunlight, increases calcium absorption. A lack of vitamin D causes rickets in children.
cards.14.key: Osteoporosis is common in women after menopause. Regular exercise strengthens bones and muscles.
cards.14.once.soru: Why might the bones of a child who never sees the sun become soft?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: Vitamin D is made in the skin with sunlight and is needed to absorb calcium.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: What softens bone is a lack of calcium.
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: Marrow makes blood cells and does not decide how hard the bone is.
cards.15.p:
• The skeleton supports and protects the body. Blood cells are made in the marrow.
• Osteoblasts build bone, and osteoclasts break it down.
• A long bone grows from its growth plate. Joints are immovable, slightly movable or movable.
• Skeletal muscle is voluntary, while smooth and cardiac muscle are involuntary.
• In contraction, actin slides, and Ca²⁺ and ATP are needed.
quiz.0.q: Match each cell with its job.
quiz.0.ciftler.1.1: Bone cell embedded in the matrix
quiz.0.ciftler.3.1: Cartilage cell living in a lacuna
quiz.0.e: An osteoblast builds bone and becomes an osteocyte once it is embedded in the matrix. An osteoclast breaks bone down. A chondrocyte is the cartilage cell that lives in a lacuna.
quiz.1.q: Put the events of a skeletal muscle contraction in order.
quiz.1.ogeler.3: Ca²⁺ binds to troponin and tropomyosin shifts
quiz.1.ogeler.5: Using ATP's energy, actin is pulled toward the middle of the sarcomere
quiz.1.e: Acetylcholine released by the motor neuron stimulates the muscle membrane. When the signal reaches the sarcoplasmic reticulum, Ca²⁺ is released. When Ca²⁺ binds to troponin, tropomyosin shifts and the binding sites open. The myosin heads attach to actin and pull it using ATP.
quiz.2.q: When a muscle contracts, what happens to the length of each structure?
quiz.2.e: The filaments do not shorten. They slide past each other. So actin, myosin and the A band, which is as long as myosin, keep their length. As actin slides to the middle, the sarcomere, the I band and the H zone get shorter.
quiz.3.q: A 15-year-old student's X-ray shows that the growth plate at the end of the femur is still open, so cartilage is visible. In their 25-year-old sister, this plate has turned to bone. What can be concluded?
quiz.3.o.0: Neither of them can grow taller anymore.
quiz.3.o.1: The sister keeps growing taller thanks to the periosteum.
quiz.3.o.2: Bone gets thicker only through the growth plate.
quiz.3.o.3: The student's long bones can still grow longer.
quiz.3.e: The bone grows longer as the cartilage in the growth plate divides. Once the plate turns to bone, growth in length stops. The bone gets thicker thanks to the periosteum.
quiz.3.y.0: The student's growth plate is still cartilage. So their bones can still grow longer.
quiz.3.y.1: The periosteum makes bone thicker, not longer. The sister, whose plate has turned to bone, can no longer grow taller.
quiz.3.y.2: The growth plate is for growth in length. Thickening happens thanks to the periosteum.
A:ozet: Watch where a bone grows from and move the joints. Bend your arm with the biceps and triceps, and see the filaments slide inside a sarcomere.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Between the diaphysis and the epiphysis there is a plate made of cartilage. Make a guess first, then press play.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Where does a bone grow longer from?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The periosteum makes the bone thicker and repairs fractures, but it does not make it longer.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Red marrow makes blood cells, and yellow marrow stores fat. Marrow does not make the bone longer.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The cartilage in the plate multiplies and turns to bone. So the bone grows at both ends. When puberty ends, the plate turns to bone and growth in height stops.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The place where bones meet is called a joint. Change the joint type and play each one. Try all three.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: In a movable joint, what lets the bone ends glide without friction?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: A tendon connects muscle to bone. It does not help the bone ends glide.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Marrow is inside the bone and makes blood cells. It has nothing to do with the joint.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The synovial fluid inside the capsule lubricates the joint, and the cartilage at the ends cushions impact. Ligaments hold the bones together.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Bend your arm at the elbow.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.ipucu: To bend the arm, the front muscle must pull and the back muscle must relax. If both contract, the arm locks.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: The biceps shortened and pulled the forearm, and the triceps relaxed. Because the muscle shortened while lifting a load, this is an isotonic contraction.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Look at the bands in the sarcomere. The A band is as long as the myosin, and the I band holds only actin. Make a guess first, then watch the contraction.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: When the muscle contracts, which one keeps its length?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The sarcomere shortens and the Z lines move closer. Its length drops from 2.4 µm to 2.0 µm.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The I band is the region that holds only actin. As actin slides inward, the I band narrows.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The A band is as long as the myosin, and myosin does not shorten. The filaments do not shorten, they slide past each other. The I band and H zone narrow.
A:adimlar.4.metin: When Ca²⁺ binds to troponin, tropomyosin shifts and the binding sites on actin open. Get the muscle ready to contract and press play.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.ipucu: Contraction needs two things: Ca²⁺ to open the binding sites and ATP to supply the pulling energy.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: The muscle contracted. Relaxing also needs ATP, because a myosin head lets go of actin only when it binds ATP. Ca²⁺ is also pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum using ATP. After death, when ATP runs out, the heads cannot let go. This is called rigor mortis.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The stored ATP in a muscle lasts only a few seconds. You just started running. Make a guess first, then press play.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: When stored ATP runs out, which source renews ATP first?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Creatine phosphate passes its phosphate to ADP right away and renews ATP. This supply also runs out in a few seconds, and then respiration takes over.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Aerobic respiration gives the most ATP, but it takes time to kick in. It powers long-lasting activity.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Fermentation works when there is not enough oxygen and gives only 2 ATP per glucose. It is not the first source after stored ATP.
A:adimlar.6.metin: The body has three types of muscle. The stripes in muscle come from the regular arrangement of actin and myosin. Look at the tissues.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: Which muscle is both striated and involuntary?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Skeletal muscle is striated, but it is voluntary. You contract it yourself.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Smooth muscle works involuntarily, as in the stomach and vessel walls, but it is not striated.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary. Intercalated discs link the cells and the signal spreads quickly.
A:kapanis.0: A bone grows longer from its growth plates, and the plate turns to bone at the end of puberty. The periosteum makes the bone thicker and repairs fractures.
A:kapanis.1: Joints are immovable, slightly movable or movable. In movable joints, synovial fluid and cartilage reduce friction.
A:kapanis.2: Muscles only pull. The biceps bends the arm, and the triceps straightens it.
A:kapanis.3: In contraction, actin and myosin do not shorten. They slide past each other. The sarcomere, the I band and the H zone shorten, while the A band stays the same.
A:kapanis.4: Contraction needs Ca²⁺ and ATP. ATP is renewed first by creatine phosphate, then by respiration.
